newsitem.title: USA: Mass. lawmakers review $22 bln of borrowing plans.
newsitem.headline: Mass. lawmakers review $22 bln of borrowing plans.

text.p: The Massachusetts House Ways and Means Committee is considering a bill this week extending the life of dozens of state projects totalling $22 billion.

Bond authorizations paying for the work, ranging from a new art museum to removing toxic wastes, were good for only five years, and expire on the last day of the fiscal year, June 30. If the bill is not passed by then, work on the projects will have to stop.

Such extension bills are routine. But the committee took an unusually careful look at this one, as members try to get a handle on how deep the state is in debt, and what that debt is buying, according to a study by State House News Service.
The state now owes bondholders $9.2 billion to repay past bond issues.
In addition, the Legislature has authorized another $13.1 billion in borrowing for various projects. Some $8.145 billion of that has been approved in just the past two-and-a-half years, including:
$120 million - Redevelopment of the former Fort Devens
This $8.145 billion is on top of $4.985 billion authorized in past years.
Total in "authorized but unissued" debt, according to the Long Term Debt Committee: $13.130 billion.
This year, lawmakers could approve at least another $1.140 billion, including:
$ 15 million- Police and fire equipment grants
$ 15 million- Redevelopment incentives for "brownfields" (contaminated urban lots)
If all that new debt is factored in, the Legislature will have approved $14.270 billion.

Besides the state's general obligation bonds, issued for courthouse improvement, new jails and all the other purposes of state government, the state guarantees or helps pay off another $3.3 billion worth of debt, for the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority, the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority, the Turnpike Authority and the Massachusetts Government Land Bank.

Even without all the debt the Legislature has approved, the state is already very close to its legal debt ceiling. That means the state has made about $4 billion more in borrowing commitments than it has the legal ability to fulfill in any given year.
The administration authorizes only $900 million worth of new borrowing each year, and pays off about the same amount in old debt.

Of course, the Legislature can raise the legal debt ceiling whenever it wants -- but that would make it much harder for the state to win an increase in its bond rating, a major goal of fiscal managers on Beacon Hill.
Moody's Investors Service rates the Commonwealth's general obligation debt A1. Standard & Poors Corp rates it A-plus, as does Fitch Investors.
